1.pericope_label: Go and get thee a linen girdle, and hide it there in a hole of the rock
debates: Whether the journey was made or seen in vision
Whether the river named is the Euphrates or Ephratah
Why the girdle was not to be put in water
outliers: Ellicott rejects the reading that the command about water was meant to preserve the girdle, and makes it a figure of guilt unwashed by repentance
Ellicott dismisses the objection drawn from the length of a double journey of two hundred and fifty miles
themes: A sign acted rather than spoken
A garment of consecration left to rot
A place chosen to name the land of exile
Length of time built into a symbol

8.pericope_label: Thus saith the LORD, After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah
debates: Whether the word at the ninth verse means pride or excellency
What the word rendered imagination means
Whether the sign takes in Judah only
outliers: Calvin stands against the unanimous rendering of the ninth verse and takes the word in a good sense, as the dignity God had given
Ellicott notes a partial reversal of this sentence in a later chapter, where the exiles are the good figs
themes: A dignity conferred and then withdrawn
Refusal of teaching counted worse than ignorance
Election described as a bond of mutual union
A confidence that swells with wind

12.pericope_label: Every bottle shall be filled with wine, and I will dash them one against another
debates: What kind of vessel is meant
Why the people took the saying for a truism
Whether the drunkenness is a reprobate mind or the calamity itself
outliers: Clarke explains the retort from the season, a promising vintage making the saying look obvious
Calvin says God chose a trifling and seemingly frivolous saying to show that the people could not perceive even what was most evident
themes: A proverb turned into a threat
Wine desired and wine given
Rank offering no exemption
Society breaking apart from within

15.pericope_label: Give glory to the LORD your God, before he cause darkness
debates: Whether giving glory means confessing guilt or acknowledging his power
Whether the verb about darkness is causative
What the mountains named are
outliers: Calvin stands alone in refusing the sense of confession here and takes the phrase as submission to the word
Ellicott shows that the word for twilight is used only of evening and never of dawn
themes: A prophet defending his commission
Pride named as the root of refusal
Light expected and darkness given
Warning withdrawn as itself a judgment

18.pericope_label: Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down
debates: Which king and queen are addressed
Whether the cities of the south are in Judah or in Egypt
What the closing words of the nineteenth verse mean
outliers: Calvin breaks with almost all interpreters and takes the cities of the south for the cities of Egypt, where the people looked for refuge
Ellicott notes that the word for the royal head-tires occurs nowhere else and may have been coined or drawn from the court vocabulary
themes: A sentence delivered to the throne itself
Teaching that respects no person
A refuge closed before it is reached
A district blockaded before the capital is attacked

20.pericope_label: Where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?
debates: Whether the summons is addressed to the king or to the people
How the twenty-first verse is to be construed
What the uncovering of the skirts and heels means
outliers: Ellicott says the twenty-first verse requires an entire retranslation and offers two constructions of it
Calvin takes the mixed numbers in the same verse as pointing first to the commander and then to the whole army
themes: A shepherd called to account for the flock
Allies taught to become masters
A question asked in the heart and answered
Pride displayed and shame displayed

23.pericope_label: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
debates: Who the people named at the twenty-third verse are
Whether the impossibility is absolute or only moral
What the word rendered measures means
outliers: Calvin refuses to let the verse be used as a proof that man has no free will, since it speaks of a habit contracted by long practice and not of nature
Keil and Delitzsch answer the argument that the word can only mean garment and never measure
themes: A fixed trait taken as the figure of a fixed habit
Difficulty distinguished from impossibility
Straw carried off by a desert wind
An inheritance exchanged for a measured portion

26.pericope_label: Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face; wilt thou not be made clean?
debates: Whether the adulteries named are literal or figurative
What the word rendered lewdness means
Whether the closing question leaves the case open
outliers: Clarke questions the human custom that lies behind the figure, asking whether it was the way to correct the evil
Clarke reads the closing question as showing that the earlier comparison stated a difficulty and not an impossibility
themes: A retaliation matched to the offence
Shame answering shame
Devotion described as an animal heat
A door left open at the end of a sentence
